analysis_notes.gap_explanation: Torah #200 has no bechina edges in torahData.js. The source text is two sentences presenting one eitza relationship (fulfilling Torah from poverty → meriting to fulfill it from wealth) mediated by the mechanism of gilgul (reincarnation). The five concepts that appear in the text — poverty-observance, wealth-observance, gilgul, contemporary tzaddikim, and earlier-generation tzaddikim — are all related causally or contextually, not through bechina (shared essential nature). The teaching does not declare any of these to be aspects of the same underlying reality; it describes a sequence: past poverty-observance is the cause; present wealth-fulfillment is the effect; gilgul is the mechanism that binds the two lifetimes into a single soul-trajectory. Therefore, even if these concepts were added to the dataset, they would produce eitza edges, not bechina edges, and would not contribute to any package formation. There are no missing bechina relationships in this Torah — the absence of bechina edges in the dataset accurately reflects the absence of bechina language in the source text.
analysis_notes.source_text_summary: Torah #200 is a brief two-sentence teaching. The opening question is: why are contemporary tzaddikim wealthy, whereas in earlier times most tzaddikim were poor and indigent? The answer: the Mishnah in Avot (4) states, 'All who fulfill the Torah from poverty will ultimately fulfill it from wealth.' The contemporary tzaddikim are — through the secret of gilgul (reincarnation) — the very same souls as the earlier tzaddikim who fulfilled the Torah from poverty. Having already fulfilled that stage of poverty-based observance in a previous lifetime, they now merit to fulfill the Mishnah's promise and serve God from a position of wealth. The entire teaching is one application of a Mishnaic eitza rule to the generational reality of the tzaddikim's economic circumstances.
structural_observations: The teaching's sole conceptual move is an eitza: קיום התורה מעוני → זכות לקיים מעושר. This is the Mishnah's own causal promise, applied across lifetimes via gilgul.

The gilgul concept functions as a bridging mechanism — it explains how a consequence promised in one lifetime (wealth) materializes in a subsequent lifetime without contradiction. It is not itself a bechina equation but a theological premise.

The good/evil polarity structure that characterizes richer Torahs is entirely absent here. There is no opposing evil dimension discussed. The teaching is a positive theological explanation with no explicit counterforce.

Torah #200 is one of the shortest and most conceptually sparse teachings in Likutay Moharan Vol. 1 — comparable in length and structure to Torah #198 (two sentences, single eitza) and Torah #195 (three lines, single implicit bechina). However, unlike Torah #195 which contains at least an implicit bechina equation, Torah #200 contains strictly eitza logic throughout.
